topic: Law of Contracts and Specific Relief: General Principles of Contract Act, 1872
description: This module covers the foundational elements of contract law under the Indian Contract Act, 1872. It outlines what transforms a mere agreement into a legally enforceable contract, detailing the essentials such as offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity, and free consent.

key_points: Definition: Section 2(h) defines a contract as 'an agreement enforceable by law.' Therefore, Contract = Agreement + Enforceability.

Essential Elements: According to Section 10, all agreements are contracts if they are made by the free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration and with a lawful object, and are not expressly declared to be void.
Offer and Acceptance: There must be a lawful proposal (offer) by one party and a lawful acceptance by the other, resulting in an agreement (consensus ad idem - meeting of minds).

Consideration (Section 2(d)): 'Quid pro quo' or something in return. A contract without consideration is generally void (nudum pactum), subject to certain exceptions like agreements made out of natural love and affection.
Capacity to Contract (Section 11): Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority, is of sound mind, and is not disqualified by law.

Minor's Agreement: In the landmark case of Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose (1903), the Privy Council established that an agreement entered into by a minor is 'void ab initio' (void from the very beginning), not merely voidable.

free_consent_and_voidability.concept: Free Consent and Flaws in Agreement
key_points: Free Consent (Section 13 & 14): Consent means agreeing upon the same thing in the same sense. It is 'free' when it is not caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, or mistake.

Voidable Contracts: If consent is obtained by Coercion (threats/force), Undue Influence (dominating will), Fraud (intentional deception), or Misrepresentation (innocent false statement), the contract is 'voidable' at the option of the aggrieved party.
Mistake (Section 20): A bilateral mistake of a crucial fact makes the agreement entirely void, whereas a unilateral mistake generally does not render the contract voidable.

mcq_bank.subtopic: Definition and Essentials of a Contract

questions.question: According to Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what constitutes a 'contract'?

options.A: Any promise made between two friends.
options.C: A written document signed by a notary.
options.D: A social invitation that is accepted.

questions.explanation: Section 2(h) explicitly defines a contract as 'an agreement enforceable by law.' Social agreements (like an invitation to dinner) are not enforceable by law and thus are not contracts.

questions.question: A 16-year-old student (a minor) signs an agreement to sell his inherited property to an adult for a large sum of money. The adult pays an advance. Later, the minor refuses to sell. Can the adult enforce this contract in court?

options.A: Yes, because the adult already paid an advance amount.
options.B: Yes, because property transactions by minors are always valid.
options.C: No, because an agreement with a minor is void ab initio (void from the beginning) and holds no legal standing.
options.D: No, unless the minor's friends act as witnesses to the agreement.

questions.explanation: Under Section 11, a minor is incompetent to contract. As established in the Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose case, any agreement with a minor is void ab initio (completely null from the start), meaning it cannot be enforced by either party.

questions.question: Person A threatens to harm Person B's family unless B sells their vintage car to A for a fraction of its true value. B, acting out of fear, signs the contract. What is the legal status of this contract?

options.A: The contract is perfectly valid because B signed the document voluntarily in the end.
options.B: The contract is voidable at the option of Person B, because B's consent was obtained by coercion.
options.C: The contract is void ab initio and cannot be enforced even if B later wants to proceed with it.
options.D: The contract is valid but A must pay the full market value of the car.

questions.explanation: This is a classic case of 'Coercion' (Section 15). When consent is obtained through coercion, the agreement is a contract 'voidable' at the option of the party whose consent was so caused (Section 19). Person B can choose to either rescind (cancel) the contract or affirm it.
